title: Bo: come, not go (Exodus 10:1)
hook: God tells Moses "come unto Pharaoh", as if God is already in the room
tomorrow: Bo: darkness that could be felt (Exodus 10:21–23)

segments.voice: Yesterday year two opened. Your line was the scroll keeps rolling. Did you pick something up where you left it? Today the scroll rolls into a new portion, and its very first word. Day three hundred thirty-three.

There's a difference between a coach who says go out there and one who says come on, out we go. Same field. Same game. But one of them is staying on the bench, and the other one is walking out beside you. Moses has stood before Pharaoh again and again. Plague after plague has come. Each time, Pharaoh ends up saying no. Moses has every reason to dread going back. And the portion opens with God sending him back, using a word that, in Hebrew, is a little strange. It isn't the word for go. It's the word for come.
screen: `GO OUT THERE, OR COME ON.` → `PLAGUE AFTER PLAGUE, STILL NO.` → `NOT GO. COME.`

segments.voice: The portion is named for that word: Bo. In Hebrew, God says to Moses, bo el Par'oh. The old Jewish translation, like the King James, smooths it into go in unto Pharaoh, and that's fair: the Hebrew verb can mean entering. But its plain sense is come. And people who speak to you as come are usually already where they're asking you to be. The Zohar, a classic work of Jewish mysticism, plays with exactly this. It pictures God leading Moses inward, room after room, into the innermost chamber of Pharaoh's power, the place Moses was most afraid of, and saying: come. Not go there alone. Come here, where I already am. It's a reading, not the plain story, and the Zohar wraps it in a lot of symbolism about the deep places of evil. But the simple point doesn't need the symbolism. Back at the burning bush, Moses had asked who he was to stand before Pharaoh. God's answer then was a short promise: "Certainly I will be with thee." Bo is that promise, folded into one syllable. It doesn't make the room less hard. Pharaoh will still say no. The verse even says, right there, that his heart has been hardened. Moses still has to walk in. He just doesn't walk in first.
screen: `BO EL PAR'OH: COME UNTO PHARAOH.` · `COME: SOMEONE IS ALREADY THERE.` · `THE ZOHAR: ROOM AFTER ROOM.` · `I WILL BE WITH THEE.` · then, large: `COME, NOT GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse a hard room. Settle, and breathe. Think of a room you're dreading this week. A meeting, a phone call, a doctor's office, a kitchen where an old argument lives. Picture the door. Now picture walking through it, not as the first one in, but as someone being called in, by a voice already inside. If you pray, you can hold the words I will be with thee as you cross the threshold. If not, just picture one person who'd be on your side in there. Stay with that doorway. The bell holds the time.
Bo. Come. The name of this week's portion, and the word God uses to send Moses back to Pharaoh, as if calling him into a room God is already in.
Your line: come, not go. Today, when you walk into the hardest room on your list, say it under your breath at the door. Day three hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Bo is read in synagogues in winter. Some teachers, Hasidic commentators among them, dwell on its first word, reading 'come' as a sign that God goes ahead of Moses into Pharaoh's palace.

match.prompt: inside the first verse — tap the pairs.

myth: the Hebrew word bo plainly means come
translations often say go in, but the simple sense is come.
after God says come, Pharaoh finally agrees
the same verse says his heart is hardened. the room stays hard.
the room-after-room picture is in the plain text of Exodus
it's the Zohar's reading, a mystical interpretation of the word bo.

fork.setup: you're Moses. plague after plague, and Pharaoh still says no. God sends you back to Pharaoh. which word does the Hebrew use?
options: come: as if God is already inside.
fork.reveal: bo: come. readers from the Zohar onward hear in it that God is already in the room Moses dreads.

original.note: Hebrew: come, or enter. the first word God speaks in the portion, and its name.

trapdoor: what you thought: God sends Moses off to Pharaoh again.
what it means: God says come, not go, as if calling Moses in from the other side of the door.
what a scholar hears: the Zohar (2:34a) reads bo as God leading Moses chamber by chamber into Pharaoh's innermost room.
